messages.author: 7a97c986864bf6d6
messages.subject: prior over NB regression predicted points - jacobian
parts:
Hello Community,

I have a negative binomial regression with log link, and I would like to put a prior on the predicted values

"e" is the predicted regression values
 
transformed parameters {
  vector<lower=0>[S] e[G,P];//the linear predictor
  for(g in 1:G) for(p in 1:P) e[g,p] = exp(X*gamma[g,p]); //using the log link 
}

"gamma" is the regression parameters and does NOT have prior on it

I would like to put

for(p in 1:P) for(g in 1:G) e[g, p] ~ gamma(alpha[p,g], beta[p,g]);

The question is do I have to add the Jacobian adjustment?

target += gamma * X


Thanks a lot.

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: prior over NB regression predicted points - jacobian
parts:
Yeah, I think you need a Jacobian here. It's Chapters 20 (section "Jacobians not Necessary" and 20.3) and 33 in the manual that cover this.

I'm assuming X is a constant [S, K] matrix, and each gamma[g, p] is a length K vector.

If K > 1, I'm not super sold on the adjustment being just a bunch of X * gammas (not clear from the model if it is or isn't).

I've just been thinking through this stuff recently myself, so take my word with a grain of salt, but, if I'm thinking clearly:

If things were scalars, we want to sample on gamma, and we have specified a distribution on exp(X * gamma), then f^-1 = exp(X * gamma), df^-1/dgamma = X * exp(X * gamma), log(abs(df^-1/dgamma)) = log(abs(X)) + X * gamma, and you could drop the log(abs(X)) because it is constant.

If you're dealing with matrices/vectors, you have a multivariate transform for each exp(X * gamma[g, p]). It's not obvious to me your Jacobian would in general be triangular or diagonal (because of the matrix product X * gamma[g, p]) so check that (Chaper 33, "Multivariate Changes of Variables").

Does that make sense at all?

Ben

for those who have access to Mathematica:

(Notes: I replaced gamma with g, to avoid confusion with the Gamma function, Re[g x] = real of g * x)

PowerExpand[Log[Abs[D[Exp[x*g], g]]]]

returns: Log[Abs[x]] + Re[g x]

Thus you calculation is right.

messages.author: 3d7541308bd2e290
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: prior over NB regression predicted points - jacobian
parts:
This looks like a glm of some sort. It looks like you're using R, so have you see Rstanarm? Check this out: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/count.html

There's a section on fitting count data with negative binomials there as well (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/count.html#poisson-and-negative-binomial-regression-example). Maybe this package will let you do your regression more easily?

But back to your model, I think the distributions on 'e' you're specifying are in a weird place. I think I agree with Andre that you've got an extra gamma distribution in there that might not need to be there. Check out: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negative_binomial_distribution#Gamma.E2.80.93Poisson_mixture . Can the gamma in this case just get integrated out? I think doing that transform specifies both parameters of the negative Poisson as well (so there's no free sigma).

Now to the Jacobians, I think the Jacobians not making sense is a result of the model.

For example, just taking three rows of your X:

X = [1, 2.0
1, 1.0
1, 0.5]

If y = Xg

y0 = g0 + 2 * g1
y1 = g0 + g1
y2 = g0 + 0.5 * g1

This means

y0 = 3 * y1 - 2 * y2

So if you specify distributions on y1 and y2, you already have a distribution on y0!

So applying the priors where you are I think is creating issues cause there are bunch of different conflicting soft constraints. I don't deeply understand the Math behind when you can easily apply the Jacobian adjustment or not, but it's not always.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior over NB regression predicted points - jacobian
parts:
> On Apr 23, 2017, at 5:41 AM, Ste <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
>
> Hello Community,
>
> I have a negative binomial regression with log link, and I would like to put a prior on the predicted values
Not a good idea as it breaks the generative nature of the model.

> "e" is the predicted regression values
>
> transformed parameters {
> vector<lower=0>[S] e[G,P];//the linear predictor
> for(g in 1:G) for(p in 1:P) e[g,p] = exp(X*gamma[g,p]); //using the log link
> }
>
> "gamma" is the regression parameters and does NOT have prior on it
>
> I would like to put
>
> for(p in 1:P) for(g in 1:G) e[g, p] ~ gamma(alpha[p,g], beta[p,g]);

No matter how you try to put a distribution on exp(X * gamma[g, p]), it
won't be a proper Bayesian prior because it involves data. Thus it breaks
the interpretation of a Bayesian model as generating parameters from the
prior and then generating data from the parameters.

If you absolutely must include constraints (usually they're a bad
idea for both statistical and computational reasons), you're better
off putting them on the gamma parameter so that the model at least
remains generative (that is, you can generate the data from the
parameters without rejection sampling!).

Or you should include them in some kind of link function.

>
> The question is do I have to add the Jacobian adjustment?
>
> target += gamma * X

If you want to put a distribution on e, then you indeed have to
apply the Jacobian. If X is a vector, you'll need to do this in
loop with X * gamma[g, p].

- Bob

parts:
Thanks Guys,

I think Bob, that indeed while the regression is my generative process, the gamma observation is generated and not generating. This discussion is getting interesting, let me show you what it does work, with tested data, outperforming current methods. The framework is not regression but grouping. Then maybe we can generalise it to continuous.


Let's suppose I have many worlds (W). In each of those, old and young people [P] (two discrete groups) have a "distinct" OR "same" number of hair ~ NB(). This could be modelled in this way:

Let young and old hair be generated by two different NB 

hair_young[p,w] ~ NB(mu_young[w], phi[w]);
hair_young[p,w] ~ NB(mu_old[w], phi[w]);

Let the two estimates mu be generated by a common Gamma

mu_young[w] ~ gamma(alpha[w], beta[w]);
mu_old[w] ~ gamma(alpha[w], beta[w]);

Now this does the trick, let those gammas for all words be generated by the same process

alpha[w] ~ gamma(a, b);
beta[w] ~ gamma(c, d);

This allows to tell apart the worlds where young and old have different number of hair. Yes because the mere difference mu_young[w]  - mu_old[w] and maybe its uncertainty (like in a frequentist approach) does NOT separate the two cases (i.e., same/  different).

But alphas and betas DO! That was for me the revelation. Because 

-- gamma generated by a age invariant process (regression y = a) in which there is no change follow a precise background alpha/beta ratio,
-- gammas generated by an age variant process  (regression y = a1 + a2 * x) have a really distinct alpha/beta ratio, having bigger variance.


Figure: mode/sd of gammas; red being age dependent

This is how I solved the hypothesis testing problem in the Bayes context, for two categories. Now this underlie a continuous generalization, but I could not crack it. What about if age is continuous and not discrete?



Thanks to all!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] prior over NB regression predicted points - jacobian
parts:
Eureka!

I found what was my misconception was in my working model. It is working but is not doing what I was thinking :)

mu_young[w] ~ gamma(alpha[w], beta[w]);
mu_old[w] ~ gamma(alpha[w], beta[w]);

is indeed not sampling the transformed (implicitly) values

mu_young = g0
mu_old = exp(g0 + g1 * x) = exp(g0) * exp(g1 * x)

but is indirectly sampling

exp(g0) ~ gamma(a1, b1);
exp(g0) * exp(g1 * x) ~ gamma(a2, b2);

therefore

exp(g1 * x) ~ gamma(a2, b2) / gamma(a1, b1);

therefore

exp(g1 * x) ~ beta_prime() OR ~ f_distribution()

references

https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/207595/distribution-of-the-ratio-of-two-gamma-random-variables
https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/143311/distribution-of-the-quotient-of-two-gamma-random-variables-with-different-rate-p


I will soon test this hypothesis and letting you know ;) This would have been a great deductive/reverse-engineering/phylosophical victory!

I did one time the gamma count distribution in Stan:
real gammacount(int y , real la, real a) {
    if(y>0)
      return gamma_p(y*a, a*la) - gamma_p((y+1)*a, a*la);
    return gamma_q((y+1)*a, a*la);
  }

target += log(y, exp(mu[i]), lambda[1]);

It uses the difference of the gamma CDF to get the PMF. 
Not tested: If you sample mu.nb ~ gamma(?!?!, a*la) you get the PDF
with la = exp(mu). Note la > 0, a > 0, a ~ gamma(b,c). 
?!?! left as homework. (Sorry I don't have time to dig into this now,
but I'm sure its not complicated.)

I don't know the full story here, but I think this is some sort of hierarchical regression problem.

You have collected hair count data for a number of different people of different ages (regression part, difference in two ages vs. continuum of ages shouldn't be that big). You have done this experiment in many different worlds, but you expect the relations to be similar (hierarchical part).

I'd start by just building that regression with Rstanarm and going from there (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/count.html, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/glmer.html).

It might be simpler to use the posteriors of the regression coefficients to analyzer your data than trying to figure out some kind of hypothesis test.

Good luck!

I don't know the full story here, but I think this is some sort of hierarchical regression problem.

You have collected hair count data for a number of different people of different ages (regression part, difference in two ages vs. continuum of ages shouldn't be that big). You have done this experiment in many different worlds, but you expect the relations to be similar (hierarchical part).

I'd start by just building that regression with Rstanarm and going from there (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/count.html, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rstanarm/vignettes/glmer.html).

It might be simpler to use the posteriors of the regression coefficients to analyzer your data than trying to figure out some kind of hypothesis test.

Good luck!
